How should I choose a cloud percentage?

Use the share of model calls that policy and capability allow in Azure. Start from data requirements, not just the cheaper model. The percentage assumes the same token mix on each route.

A hybrid system keeps both environments available, so reducing Azure calls does not automatically reduce fixed search, hosting or network charges. Disable or resize those services explicitly. Learn how workload becomes usage →

— Azure calls— local calls

Routing changes model token charges. Included provisioned infrastructure keeps billing even with no requests. Service quantities below are separate, explicit assumptions.

How do I deploy a local-only solution?

Local only is a costing scenario, not a deployment action. It excludes cloud service lines and Azure model-token charges, while enabled local and shared costs remain. It does not stop existing Azure resources.

For deployment, choose an on-device Windows application using Foundry Local or a Linux server using a dedicated inference runtime. Both need local application, identity, models and data services. Read the Windows and Linux deployment guide →

How do I estimate tokens and model calls?

Run a small set of real, representative tasks. Record total input, output and model calls, then divide by the number of calls or tasks. Include system instructions, conversation history, retrieved passages and tool messages.

If one task takes a planning call, a tool-review call and an answer call, enter three model calls per task. Billed reasoning is already part of output. For different task types, create separate saved scenarios. Walk through the $33 token example →

Why are there so many different units?

Azure charges different resources in different ways. App Service and AI Search use provisioned time. Logs and transfer use GB. OCR uses pages. Blob operations use groups of 10,000. The engine converts each quantity into its own billing unit before multiplying by price.

Expand a component to see its input quantities, source meter, rate and exact calculation. Change its frequency to one-time for initial processing where appropriate. Add omitted services explicitly. One Search replica is an example, not an availability guarantee.

Free grants default to zero available allocation. Enter only the allowance remaining for this solution at the subscription or billing-account scope. The engine prevents allocating a shared grant twice beyond its limit.

What changes when I already own the hardware?

Uncheck “Purchase this hardware now” to exclude a new purchase from upfront cash. Keep an allocated asset value so the monthly ownership comparison still includes amortization and maintenance.

Power uses average measured watts and powered hours, not just active working days. The PUE multiplier adds cooling and facility power. A $4,000 asset over 36 months allocates $111.11 per month; that amount is not added to the cash budget again.

Hardware value should include the GPU/CPU server, storage, network equipment and spares allocated to this solution. No residual value or hardware replacement is assumed. Monthly amortization is a planning allocation, not tax accounting.

Operations, licences and setup

People, local services and one-time implementation.

Which business costs should I include?

Count operations, support, local software, licences, backups, connectivity and the staff time allocated to this solution. Use one-time lines for setup, migration and rollout. Select the currency printed on your quote; the engine converts it consistently.

Leave a required price blank while you obtain a quote. The calculator will show a partial estimate instead of silently treating that cost as zero. Avoid entering maintenance or support both here and in the hardware percentage.

Add any services your design needs: identity licences, WAF/firewall/NAT/DNS, Content Safety, databases, backups, security plans, support, additional model groups or local software. An enabled line with usage and no price makes the estimate incomplete.

BUSINESS CASE + COST METHODOLOGY

How the whole-solution costing works.

Connect business demand to an explainable AI budget. Understand the decisions, cost drivers and assumptions behind every total.

Edit solution inputs →

From an AI pilot to a funded operating service

A business planning guide for sponsors, finance, architects and operations teams.

A low price per model call is not the same as a low-cost production solution. Search, document ingestion, gateways, private connectivity, monitoring, local equipment and support can outweigh token charges, especially when provisioned services run continuously at low utilization.

This calculator brings those layers into one forecast so you can compare cloud-only, local-only and hybrid approaches, distinguish upfront cash from recurring costs, and explain a funding request with traceable assumptions. It is a planning tool, not an Azure quote, invoice or capacity guarantee.

Start with a business outcome: faster document review, less time searching for knowledge, improved service turnaround or more capacity for employees. A cheaper design is not a better investment if it misses quality, latency, security or availability requirements.

Explore 10 AI cost use cases to connect your business workflow to the right measurements, calculator inputs and success criteria.

Business sponsors and product owners

Define who will use the service, how often, and what a successful task means. Use the forecast to assess affordability, adoption assumptions and the funding required to move from pilot to production.

Typical scenarios include employee knowledge assistants, document-processing workflows and AI services at intermittently connected sites.

Finance, FinOps and procurement

Review recurring cash, initial investment, reserve, equipment allocation and unit economics separately. Check contract rates, currencies and exclusions before approving a budget.

Compare low, expected and high demand scenarios. Save the assumptions and evidence with the decision record rather than sharing a total without its basis.

Architecture and operations teams

Measure call patterns and token usage, size every supporting component, and include licences, maintenance and operating effort. Test local throughput and concurrency rather than assuming hardware capacity.

Cloud-routing percentages change the model subtotal, not every infrastructure quantity. Resize search, ingestion, networking and hosting explicitly.

A practical planning and approval workflow

Use the same workload and service expectations when comparing alternatives.

  1. Define the business task, target users, success criteria, accountable owner and service requirements.
  2. Measure representative calls, prompt and output tokens, retries, document volume and retrieval activity from a pilot. One business task can require several model calls.
  3. Build low, expected and high demand scenarios. Change adoption, call counts, token sizes and service quantities deliberately; sensitivity analysis is not generated automatically.
  4. Choose cloud, local or hybrid routing, then price every required service, equipment item and operating activity. Remove components your design does not use.
  5. Review the audit trail with finance and engineering. Export the full solution CSV and save scenario JSON with an owner, review date and approval assumptions.
  6. After launch, reconcile the same resource scope and time period with Azure Cost Management, invoices, local expenses and operational metrics.

The six steps below use your current inputs. The worked business example further down is a separate, fixed illustration, not a projection of your current scenario.

1

Calculate activity and route it

Users × tasks per day × days gives monthly tasks. Multiply by model calls per task, then apply the cloud percentage. Local calls consume local capacity without a cloud token charge.

—
2

Price the Azure token categories

Cloud input is split into ordinary, cache reads and separately priced writes. Each category and output is tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × its rate. Reasoning is included once in output.

—
3

Price each service in its billing unit

Usage after an allocated free grant ÷ billing-unit size × price. Time-based capacity uses provisioned hours; daily registry meters use days. Volume bands are calculated progressively.

—
4

Add local running costs

Power = devices × watts ÷ 1,000 × hours × PUE × electricity price. Maintenance = asset value × annual percentage ÷ 12. Add licences, support and operational labour.

—
5

Keep cash and amortization distinct

Monthly operating cash sums recurring costs. Monthly allocated cost adds asset value ÷ useful life. Upfront cash includes new hardware once plus one-time service lines; existing hardware adds no new purchase.

—
6

Build the planning budget

Reserve applies to monthly operating cash. Year 1 cash = upfront + 12 × monthly budget. The horizon uses the chosen number of months. Depreciation is not added to cash again.

—

What makes the estimate complete?

Every enabled component with billable usage needs a rate. Missing rates are shown as unpriced, and final totals are withheld. A zero rate is an explicit assumption, never a substitute for a missing price.

Completeness means the selected lines are priced. It does not prove that every required architectural service has been included.

Worked example: an employee knowledge assistant

ILLUSTRATIVE USD ASSUMPTIONS

Assume 100 employees complete 10 tasks per day on 22 active days, with one model call per task, 2,000 input tokens, 500 output tokens and 80% cloud routing. Use custom input and output rates of $0.25 and $2.00 per million tokens, with no caching. These are illustrative rates, not a quote for a named model or the hosting bill for this website.

Add $150/month for cloud infrastructure, $50/month for local support and software, and $1,000 in one-time implementation. Purchase two local devices at $1,500 each and allocate their value over 36 months. Each draws 100 watts for 730 hours/month, with PUE 1.2, electricity at $0.15/kWh and annual maintenance at 12% of asset value. Apply a 20% planning reserve.

The cloud model charge is only $26.40 of $282.68 in monthly operating cash in this example. Optimizing token prices alone misses most of the operating cost. Full-precision calculations are rounded for display, so multiplying displayed amounts can produce small rounding differences. Hardware purchase cash is counted once; amortization is not added to cash budgets again.

Translate cost into a business case

Estimate potential hours saved as monthly tasks x minutes saved per task / 60. Multiply by a loaded hourly cost and a realistic realization percentage to assess usable capacity value.

Time saved is not automatically payroll savings. Account for adoption, answer quality, human review, rework and whether released capacity is redeployed or actually reduces spending. Validate benefits in a pilot; this application does not calculate ROI or payback.

Use cash budgets for funding and allocated costs for economic comparisons. Cost per planned task is not cost per successful outcome: adjust the denominator separately when failures or human intervention matter.

Keep comparisons decision-ready

The Model costs tab prices the full workload; its comparison table excludes infrastructure and equipment. The solution engine routes the model subtotal and adds active cost layers. It excludes the model tab's other charges and allowance to avoid double counting.

Routing applies the same cloud percentage to calls, input and output. Use separate scenarios when cloud and local requests have different token profiles. Lower cloud usage does not automatically reduce provisioned service costs.

The planning horizon assumes a constant monthly run rate and no automatic equipment replacement, demand growth, inflation or financing. Local-only costing is not proof of hardware capacity or a certified disconnected deployment.

Commercial, currency and information-handling guardrails

Know what has been priced and what still needs a business decision.

  • Azure presets are a dated USD retail snapshot, with East US 2 reference meters and the selected model deployment tariffs. The app's Central US hosting region does not change those reference prices. Verify regional eligibility, quota, model versions and contract terms.
  • Taxes, negotiated discounts, support agreements and unlisted services need explicit treatment. A fully priced selection is not proof that every required architectural component has been included.
  • Provisioned hours, service replicas and billing-unit conversions matter. A 730-hour month is a planning convention, not the length of every calendar month. Allocate shared plans and remaining free grants consistently rather than charging or claiming them more than once.
  • Whole-solution costs normalize to USD before reporting conversion. ECB snapshot rates or your overrides are planning rates, not guaranteed invoice exchange rates. Changing custom-rate currency in the Model costs tab relabels entered numbers without converting them.
  • Existing equipment can have no new purchase cash while still carrying power, maintenance, support and amortization. The equipment allocation is a planning convention, not accounting or tax advice.
  • Inputs are processed in the browser; the app does not connect to your Azure account or refresh prices automatically. Normal hosting request logs can still exist. The site is public: avoid confidential labels and protect exported scenarios, custom prices and screenshots.

For the full business guide and source code, see the GitHub README. Return to the solution cost engine to apply these assumptions to your scenario.

EVERY NUMBER EXPLAINED

The model calculation, step by step.

This section explains the Model costs tab before applying the solution’s cloud-routing share. All rates are per 1,000,000 tokens.

1

Turn activity into model calls

Monthly tasks = users × tasks per user per day × active days. Model calls = tasks × average calls per task.

2

Calculate total input and output

Multiply model calls by average tokens per call. Include instructions, history, retrieved text and tools in input; include billed reasoning in output.

3

Split input into billing categories

Cache reads and separately priced writes are subsets of total input. Subtract them once to get ordinary input.

4

Apply the price to each category

Category cost = tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × rate. Add ordinary input, cache reads, cache writes and output.

5

Add services and a planning reserve

Base cost = model cost + other charges. Add the chosen allowance to the entire base. This reserve is your assumption, not an Azure charge.

6

Project the year and unit costs

Annual budget = monthly budget × 12, assuming unchanged rates and use. Per-task and per-user figures use model token costs only.

Itemized token calculation

USD
Tokens divided by one million multiplied by price per million
Billing categoryMonthly tokensPrice / 1MCalculationMonthly cost

How do I compare this estimate with actual Azure charges?+

Run representative requests and record the API's usage fields. Divide measured token totals by model calls to replace the averages above. Use the same model, version, deployment, currency and reporting period.

Token categoryChat CompletionsResponses API
Total inputusage.prompt_tokensusage.input_tokens
Cache readsusage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokensusage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens
Output, including reasoningusage.completion_tokensusage.output_tokens

For supported newer Azure OpenAI models, the caching documentation also reports usage.prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens. Use provider-specific usage fields for other model families. Reasoning counts are already included in billed output; do not add them again.

In Azure Monitor, sum InputTokens, OutputTokens and TotalTokens over the same deployment and dates. In Azure Cost Management, select the correct resource or resource-group scope and group by Meter. Cost Management meter records and invoices establish actual billed cost; a price snapshot and forecast do not. Monitoring guide ↗ · Cost Management guide ↗

How do short-context and long-context prices work?+

Some models have separate tariffs based on the input length of each request. Select the tier that matches the threshold documented for your model. Monthly token totals and input-plus-output totals do not determine the tier.

If your workload mixes short and long requests, calculate those groups separately and add the costs. An average can hide requests that cross a pricing threshold. The calculator exposes explicit tier choices; it does not guess a threshold from a model's maximum context window. Azure model and context guidance ↗

What else affects my final bill?+

The Model costs tab covers text token costs using the selected Global PAYG rate schedule. PTU capacity, batch, priority processing, fine-tuning, managed compute, image, audio and video pricing use other rules. The Solution cost engine adds hosting, search, storage, embeddings, document processing, networking, monitoring, local equipment and operational costs. Add custom lines for any remaining services.

Taxes and negotiated discounts are not applied automatically. The Solution cost engine converts prices using its displayed FX snapshot or your override. Published model presets stay in USD; the model worksheet’s custom currency labels the rates you enter. Custom rates can represent your own agreement. HYBRID REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE

Two environments. One application contract.

Azure handles permitted online work. The local path has its own inference, retrieval, identity and operations so it can run disconnected.

Hybrid scenario

Hybrid AI platform: Azure online + on-premises offline

Your supplied API-driven architecture reference, preserved without changes.

Conceptual reference supplied by the project owner, not an Azure-certified deployment blueprint. Provider and model names, API support, licensing and service availability must be verified. Offline operation requires a locally complete application, identity, models and data path; Teams and other cloud clients still need connectivity. Do not assume that cloud model weights or cloud gateways can run disconnected.

Local-only deployment: Windows devices or Linux servers

A runbook for the AI application you are planning, separate from hosting this calculator.

Selecting Local only sets the model's cloud share to zero and excludes cloud-domain lines from the estimate. Enabled local and shared lines still apply. It does not deploy a model, connect this calculator to an inference endpoint, shut down Azure resources or make the public Azure website available offline.

Every dependency in the disconnected request path must be local: application UI, orchestration, identity, model runtime and files, embeddings, documents, indexes, secrets and monitoring. Prepare while connected, then test with internet access blocked.

Choose an on-device or server-based local AI deployment
DecisionWindows / on-deviceLinux / shared server
Primary fitAI embedded in a user's own desktop applicationA local application serving multiple concurrent users
Inference approachFoundry Local SDK; optional local REST serverDedicated runtime such as vLLM on supported hardware
Capacity evidenceModel fit and latency on each supported device classMeasured memory, throughput, concurrency and recovery capacity
Application boundaryDevice-local UI, runtime and required dataLocal gateway, identity and persistent data services

Path A: Windows with Foundry Local

  1. Check supported Windows, hardware, driver and SDK requirements in Microsoft's current quickstart. Choose a permitted model that fits the device's memory and quality requirements.
  2. Use the Windows-specific Foundry Local SDK package in your application. Follow the official sample to initialize the runtime, discover execution providers, download and register them, acquire the model, and generate a response.
  3. Complete model and execution-provider acquisition while connected. Pin approved versions and retain required local assets. First-run downloads are not an offline deployment strategy.
  4. Integrate inference into the actual desktop application using the SDK. If other local processes need REST, use the optional local server and its configured endpoint; do not assume an older CLI command or fixed port applies to every SDK release.
  5. Stage local documents, the embedding model, a compatible index, required OCR and configuration. Ensure identity, licences and secrets remain usable without cloud refresh.
  6. Validate cold start, a complete task, retrieval, error handling and restart without internet. Record device-specific latency, memory and quality before rollout.

Foundry Local is optimized for on-device use, typically one user per device. It is not a general-purpose multi-user server inference stack. No Azure subscription is needed for local inference, but hardware, licences, maintenance, deployment and support still have costs.

Microsoft Foundry Local quickstart · Current SDK reference

Path B: Linux with dedicated inference

  1. Select a supported Linux, accelerator, driver and runtime combination. Benchmark the chosen model and quantization against expected context lengths and concurrent users; there is no universal RAM or GPU sizing rule.
  2. While connected, stage a pinned runtime environment or container image and the complete approved model, tokenizer, configuration and chat template. Confirm licences and redistribution rights. Keep an offline package or image source for rebuilds.
  3. For a compatible vLLM installation, start from the local model directory, not a remote model identifier. The example below assumes the model is already present and the runtime is installed; replace the directory with your approved path.
# Run on the Linux inference host after staging the model and runtime.
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
export TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
vllm serve /srv/models/approved-instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8001 \
  --served-model-name local-assistant

The example binds inference to loopback. A gateway on the same host can use http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1. If the gateway is in a container or on another host, use an explicit private container or LAN route with firewall rules, TLS and authentication; that container's loopback is not the host's loopback.

Deploy the application and gateway separately. Add local document storage, a vector store such as Qdrant or pgvector when required, a matching embedding model, secrets and local identity. Configure service supervision, persistent volumes, startup order, health checks, logs, backups and recovery. Do not expose an unauthenticated inference port publicly.

Environment flags help prevent model-hub downloads but do not prove the whole system is offline. Confirm model-specific API and chat-template support, and block outbound access during acceptance testing.

vLLM serving documentation · Serving command reference

Host this calculator locally as well

Transfer this repository's files and a supported Node.js 24 LTS runtime to the device or local server. From the project directory, run the command below and open http://localhost:8080. The calculator needs no npm dependencies or build step.

node server.cjs

The Node host binds to 0.0.0.0, not only loopback. Use OS firewall rules to restrict single-device access. For a shared LAN service, use a local HTTPS reverse proxy and the required access controls; allow only the intended network.

This serves the calculator and its bundled price evidence offline. It does not provide a chat UI or wire inference, retrieval or authentication into an AI application. Update price and exchange-rate snapshots through a controlled review process.

Offline acceptance and cost checklist

  • Disconnect internet, cold-start the device or server, authenticate locally and complete a representative request with retrieval.
  • Test missing models, failed local capacity, denied document permissions, restart and backup restoration. Queue or reject restricted work; never silently fall back to cloud inference.
  • Verify that external model hubs, CDNs, cloud identity refresh, remote fonts, registries and cloud OCR are not required by the application.
  • Record model version, runtime or image digest, hardware, throughput, latency, test results, operating owner and update or rollback procedure.
  • In the cost plan, enter equipment count, purchase timing, useful life, measured watts, powered hours, PUE, electricity and maintenance.
  • Add local licences, storage, backup, monitoring, support labour and one-time implementation. Retain valid shared costs; investigate real Azure charges separately before decommissioning resources.

Offline operation requires a local app or locally served interface. Cloud clients such as Teams still need connectivity.

Map the architecture to its cost.

Select a block to see what it does, how it is billed, and which calculator inputs to adjust.

Offline means locally complete

Pre-stage models, runtimes, dependencies, credentials, documents and local indexes. Cloud authentication, cloud search and Azure-hosted orchestration cannot be required in the disconnected request path.

Policy-restricted data stays local. If local capacity is unavailable, reject or queue the request rather than silently routing it to the cloud.

Model and embedding compatibility

Choose local models with the appropriate weights, licence and hardware support. A Foundry cloud model does not automatically have a downloadable local equivalent.

Use the same embedding model for indexing and querying each vector store. If the two environments use different embedding models, rebuild each index from approved source documents.

Azure vectorization guidance ↗

Choose the right local runtime

Foundry Local is designed for on-device applications. A shared inference server needs a runtime and capacity plan suited to concurrent users. Hardware sizing here is an assumption until benchmarked.

This diagram uses an independent local gateway. Azure API Management’s self-hosted gateway has its own tier and temporary-disconnection constraints.

Foundry Local documentation ↗ · Gateway constraints ↗

BUSINESS WORKFLOW TO COST MODEL

Plan the use case, not just the model.

These are planning guides, not prefilled scenarios. Opening an input link keeps your current values. Outcome-based unit costs require a separate calculation; the app shows operating cost per planned task.

Use case 01 · customer operations

Customer support and service agents

Estimate the cost of resolving a customer case, not just generating one answer. Multi-turn conversations, retrieval, tool calls and escalations can change the economics of automation.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure cases per month, turns and model calls per case, conversation-history tokens, retries, tool fees and the share resolved without rework. Add gateway, search, logging and human-review effort where in scope.

Use one task per case and average calls across all attempts. Include paid tool/API requests and human handling as custom recurring lines. Do not add a second retry allowance if measured calls already include retries.

Compare in-scope operating cost per successfully resolved case at a fixed service quality and response time. A higher containment rate is not a saving if poor answers increase repeat contacts.

Set support workload assumptions · Add review and tool costs

Use case 02 · enterprise knowledge

Employee knowledge and RAG assistants

Budget for answers grounded in internal documents. Search capacity, document ingestion and embedding refresh can outweigh generation costs when adoption is low.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure questions, retrieved-context tokens, document changes, embedding tokens, search replicas and partitions, storage and ingestion operations. Separate initial indexing from recurring refreshes.

Enter generation in the workload, then size search, embeddings and document services explicitly. Record initial ingestion as a one-time line when appropriate. Changing cloud share does not resize those services automatically.

Track cost per accepted, grounded answer, retrieval quality and freshness. Validate whether reducing context or capacity preserves answer quality before claiming a saving.

Size retrieval and ingestion · Compare generation models

Use case 03 · document operations

Invoice, claims and document processing

Estimate the cost of turning documents into accepted business records. OCR, extraction, validation, exception handling and retention are separate parts of the workflow.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure documents and pages, scanned versus digital content, model calls, extraction tokens, storage retention and the manual-review share. Use representative short and long documents.

Represent one document as a task. For a machine-driven queue, you can use one workload user and documents per day as tasks, documenting that convention. Enter billed pages separately; do not treat a document as one OCR page.

The included Document Intelligence Read meter is not a universal price for layout or prebuilt extraction. Use the exact supported meter or a custom rate. Track cost per accepted document, correction effort and turnaround time.

Set document throughput · Add document service quantities

Use case 04 · workflow automation

Multi-step agents and business automation

Cost a completed workflow such as onboarding, reconciliation or case preparation. Planning, tool execution, validation and recovery can require several model calls per task.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure the full call chain, failed attempts, retries, prompt growth, paid tools, sandbox compute and approval effort. Include hard cases and incomplete runs, not only successful demonstrations.

Use average total model calls per business task and add custom tool, worker-compute and review lines. For multiple models with different tariffs, use separate model scenarios rather than applying one model's rate to every step.

Track cost per correctly completed workflow and completion rate. Runtime limits, spend caps and human approval policies must be enforced by the real application; this calculator does not enforce them.

Model agent call counts · Add workflow operating costs

Use case 05 · software engineering

Coding assistants and code-review agents

Evaluate API-based coding assistance using accepted changes and review outcomes, not generated lines of code. Repository context and repeated test-and-repair loops can dominate usage.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure tasks per engineer, repository-context tokens, billed output including reasoning, review calls, retries and test-runner or sandbox usage. Track acceptance, correctness and review effort.

Use the workload and model comparison for API consumption. Add indexing, build runners, storage and review labour separately. Seat-based assistant licences are custom service costs, not automatically equivalent to token billing.

Compare cost per accepted, tested change or reviewed pull request at comparable quality. Apply the correct context tariff and count reasoning only once in billed output.

Inspect model and context tariffs · Add licences and build costs

Use case 06 · high-volume processing

Batch classification and summarization

Estimate asynchronous tagging, catalogue enrichment or large-scale summarization when jobs can tolerate a completion window rather than interactive latency.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure items, tokens per item, failed or reprocessed jobs, queue storage, worker hours and delivery deadlines. Compare a normal processing cycle with a backlog-clearing scenario.

Use one task per item and explicit calls per task. Batch pricing, eligibility, quotas and completion guarantees are not implied by the Global PAYG presets. Enter verified batch/contract rates as custom rates in a separate scenario.

Track cost per accepted item and completion within the required window. Compare like-for-like totals; do not apply an assumed batch discount on top of a rate that already includes it.

Enter the applicable custom rates · Set item volume and calls

Use case 07 · voice experiences

Voice assistants and contact-centre analytics

Separate speech, language-model reasoning and voice output when planning voice services. Audio processing does not become a complete estimate by entering transcript tokens alone.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure billed audio minutes or tokens, transcription, generated speech, text-model calls, telephony, recordings and retention. Reconcile each quantity to the exact service's billing unit.

The model engine is a text-token estimator, not a native audio-pricing engine. Add transcription, speech synthesis, telephony and storage as custom lines using verified units and prices. If a tariff bundles modalities, avoid counting the same charge twice.

Track cost per analyzed audio hour or successfully completed voice interaction, alongside latency and transcription quality. Real-time throughput and concurrency require separate testing.

Add speech and telephony meters · Model the text-processing workload

Use case 08 · multimodal operations

Image analysis and video inspection

Plan product-image checks, visual document review or inspection workflows using the actual image or video tariff and the expected review workload.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure images, frames, resolution or detail level, modality-specific token counts, video processing, storage, transfer and human verification. Sample difficult cases as well as typical ones.

The calculator does not infer image or video billing from file count, resolution or duration. Enter measured billable tokens only when they match the selected tariff, or add explicit custom modality lines. Count follow-up text generation separately only when it is separately billed.

Track cost per validated image or inspected video hour and the false-accept/reject rate. A text-only model preset is not proof that the required vision feature or pricing is supported.

Add explicit image/video cost lines · Review storage and data transfer

Use case 09 · local and edge AI

Branch, retail and industrial edge assistants

Compare local or hybrid delivery for sites with intermittent connectivity or data-location constraints. Zero Azure model-token charges do not mean zero operating cost.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure devices per site, inference utilization, peak concurrency, power, maintenance, model updates, local storage and support visits. Include rollout and recovery effort across the fleet.

Use Local only or Hybrid, then enter equipment purchase timing, useful life, power and local service lines. Hardware fields describe a homogeneous group; use separate scenarios for different device classes and reconcile shared costs once.

Track cost per site and successful local task, together with offline availability. Capacity, licences, fully local identity and recovery must be validated; the calculator does not deploy or benchmark the runtime.

Price local equipment · Review local deployment requirements

Use case 10 · quality and governance

Model evaluation and release assurance

Budget for the work needed to choose, test and safely maintain an AI system. Evaluation runs, model judges and recurring regression tests are not free overhead.

Cost drivers, inputs and success measures

Measure test cases, candidates, repeated runs, judge calls, token usage, test compute, trace retention and expert review. Separate initial selection from recurring release checks.

Model each candidate or judge tariff separately when needed. Add compute, observability and reviewer time as custom lines. Label initial evaluation as one-time and release testing as recurring according to your actual cadence.

Track cost per accepted release or qualified candidate against explicit quality thresholds. This application does not run evaluations, calculate model accuracy or automate governance approval.

Compare candidate model costs · Budget evaluation and reviewer effort

Turn a use case into a comparable business case

Keep workload, service quality, time period and cost basis consistent.

  1. Define the task and a measurable successful outcome. Include failed attempts and rework in the costs, not just successful requests.
  2. Collect measured quantities, then create low, expected and high demand scenarios. Compare call counts, token sizes, capacity and human effort without changing every assumption at once.
  3. Separate one-time rollout or ingestion from steady-state operations. Assign custom lines to their cloud, local or shared environment. Preserve fixed services that remain provisioned even when adoption is low.
  4. Calculate outcome unit cost separately as the selected in-scope cost divided by successful outcomes in the same period. Compare cash budgets for funding or allocated costs for economic decisions; do not mix them.
  5. Save scenario JSON and export CSV evidence. When combining use cases, allocate shared hosting, search, grants and operations once rather than adding several full-stack budgets blindly.

One scenario uses one model tariff and one average workload. The app does not automatically load use-case presets, combine model portfolios, calculate ROI, model demand growth or enforce spending caps. Unpriced custom costs must be resolved before treating a forecast as decision-ready.

Lesson 1

Understand what a token measures

A token is a piece of text processed by a model. It can be a word, part of a word or punctuation. Token counts vary with the model, language and content; a word count is only a rough starting point.

Input tokens include the question, instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents and tool results sent to the model. Output tokens cover generated content. A short question can therefore have a large input bill when your app attaches many documents.

Deep dive: reasoning and caching

Azure OpenAI reasoning models bill reasoning tokens as output, even when they do not appear in the visible answer. If reported output already includes reasoning, do not add it again. See Microsoft’s reasoning-token guide.

A cache read reuses eligible input computation at the selected model’s cache-read rate. Cache-write fees and eligibility vary by model. Use measured cache hits; repetition does not guarantee a hit. Classify each usage quantity according to its rate card so it is not counted twice. See Azure prompt caching.

Lesson 2

Count tasks, then count model calls

A task is what a person wants done, such as answering a support question. A model call is one request to a model. An agent might plan, search, review a tool result and draft an answer using several calls for one task.

Monthly calls = active users × tasks per user per day × active days × average model calls per task. Include billable retry attempts in the average model calls per task. Do not add retries again if your measured calls already include them.

Deep dive: replace guesses with measurements

Run representative tasks and record input, cached input, output, calls and successful outcomes. Include simple, typical and difficult examples. Calculate averages for each task type, then weight them by expected traffic. A support answer and a long document review should not automatically share one token average.

Use a typical scenario and a busy scenario. Check peak concurrency and latency separately: monthly token totals alone do not establish whether a deployment can keep up.

Lesson 3

Follow a complete token-cost example

This example uses the included GPT-5 mini USD snapshot: $0.25 per million input tokens and $2.00 per million output tokens. It assumes no cache savings, no retries and one model call per task. Check the model tab’s date and deployment details before reusing these rates; they are not your negotiated contract.

Example monthly workload and model cost
StepCalculationResult
Model calls100 users × 10 tasks × 22 days × 1 call22,000 calls
Input usage22,000 × 2,000 tokens44 million tokens
Input charge44 × $0.25$11.00
Output usage22,000 × 500 tokens11 million tokens
Output charge11 × $2.00$22.00
Model total$11.00 + $22.00$33.00
What changes if 80% of calls use Azure?

With the same token mix, Azure processes 17,600 calls. Its model charge becomes $33.00 × 80% = $26.40. The remaining 4,400 local calls still need hardware, electricity and operations. Add cloud and local infrastructure to obtain the solution total. A routing percentage does not automatically turn off either environment.

Source reference: Azure OpenAI pricing.

Lesson 4

Price every service in its own unit

The general rule is cost = billable quantity ÷ pricing unit × unit price. Keep the units aligned: 2 million tokens at a price per million means two pricing units. A price per 1,000 operations is different from a price per operation.

Examples of quantities to measure
ComponentQuantity
Generation and embeddingsTokens, with separate applicable rates
Compute and search capacityProvisioned instances or units × hours
Documents and storageProcessed pages, GB-month and operations
Logs and networkingIngested or transferred GB, plus applicable fixed charges
Deep dive: flat prices, tiers and free grants

A flat rate applies one price to the eligible quantity. Progressive pricing applies different prices to successive bands; do not apply the cheapest band to all usage. Subtract a confirmed free allowance only once, at its actual account, service and time-period scope. An allowance may already be used by another workload.

Read the meter’s region, deployment type and unit. Embedding documents during ingestion and embedding search questions are separate usage. Azure’s embedding guide explains this retrieval dependency.

Lesson 5

Separate running cost, purchase cost and budget

Operating cost pays for ongoing cloud services, electricity, support and staff time. Upfront cost pays for purchases and initial implementation. Local inference can avoid an API token charge while still carrying both kinds of cost.

A forecast is your best estimate. A budget may include a reserve: $1,000 forecast × 1.20 = $1,200 budget. That extra $200 is your 20% contingency, not an Azure service fee or a prediction that it will be spent.

Deep dive: amortization without double counting

For planning, a $12,000 server allocated across 36 months contributes about $333.33 per month, assuming no residual value. This allocation helps compare ownership with recurring cloud costs; it does not change when you pay the supplier.

Use monthly operating cost plus allocation for an economic comparison. Use hardware purchases plus implementation plus operating payments for a cash plan. Do not include the full purchase and its monthly allocation in the same total. App Service plan billing also illustrates why provisioned platform capacity remains a separate cost.

Lesson 6

Compare scenarios and choose a reporting currency

The sourced Azure rates use USD. A reporting currency converts the estimate for discussion: reporting amount = USD amount × reporting-currency units per USD. Record the exchange-rate date and source, or label a manually entered rate as an assumption.

Conversion does not select a different Azure region, retrieve a local Azure price list or reproduce your billing agreement. Follow the currency label on hardware and other manual inputs; an INR amount entered in a USD field changes the estimate incorrectly.

Deep dive: make a fair cloud/local comparison

Compare the same task volume, quality requirements and operating period. Keep fixed cloud and local services enabled when they are still required. Change one assumption at a time to understand its effect, then compare complete scenarios.

Results are financial estimates, not hardware sizing or capacity validation. Confirm model fit, measured throughput, availability and data-routing policy separately. Offline operation also needs local retrieval, identity and secrets; see Foundry Local’s deployment scope.

Plain-language glossary

Token
A small unit processed by a model.
Input tokens
Content sent into a model call.
Output tokens
Generated tokens counted by the provider.
Reasoning tokens
Internal generated work; check output billing.
Cache read
Reuse of eligible previously processed input.
Cache write
Creating reusable cached input; fees vary.
Task
One user goal or business activity.
Model call
One request to a model endpoint.
Retry
Another attempt after an unsuccessful request.
RAG
Retrieving information to supply to a model.
Embedding
A numeric representation used for similarity search.
Rate
The price for a defined billing unit.
Billing unit
The amount covered by one quoted price.
Free grant
An eligible allowance with limits and scope.
Fixed cost
Cost retained while provisioned capacity is kept.
Variable cost
Cost that changes with measured consumption.
Upfront cost
Purchase or setup cash paid initially.
Amortization
Allocating a purchase across a planning period.
Reserve
Extra budget for uncertain future spending.
Reporting FX
An exchange rate used to display the estimate.

Questions people usually ask

Can I price audio, images or video with the text-token presets?

Not automatically. Use the exact service's billing quantities and rates in custom cost lines, or measured tokens only when they match the tariff. Add speech, image, video, telephony and associated storage charges explicitly, without counting bundled charges twice.

How do I estimate a workflow that uses several models?

Use separate scenarios for different model tariffs or workloads, then reconcile the results outside the app. Sum each model's consumption once and allocate shared infrastructure, grants and operations once. Adding complete solution budgets without that reconciliation can double count costs.

Why could my Azure invoice differ?

Actual usage, price dates, regional meters, negotiated terms, taxes, allowances and currency treatment may differ. Reconcile usage and meter identifiers before comparing totals.

Why does reducing cloud traffic not remove all cloud cost?

Provisioned compute, search and networking can remain enabled. Review those quantities separately from token consumption.

Is the lowest token price the best choice?

Compare cost per successful task. Extra calls, retries or longer answers can offset a cheaper token rate. Test quality with your own examples.

Does this budget stop my services at the limit?

No. This calculator estimates spending; it does not enforce a spending cap or change your Azure resources.

When should I update the estimate?

Before a purchasing decision and whenever traffic, model, deployment, rates or architecture changes. Replace assumptions with measured usage as it becomes available.
